title: Integral surjective base change on the target
statement:
With $f:X\to S$ and $n$ as in [sbc-def-base-change-property] assume for
some $q\geq1$ that $\mathrm{BC}(f,n,q-1)$ holds universally (in the
single degree $q-1$, which is all that [sbc-lem-bc-injectivity]
needs).
Consider commutative
diagrams

$$
\begin{array}{ccccccc}
X & \xleftarrow{\;\;} & X' & \xleftarrow{h} & Y & \xleftarrow{\pi'} & Y'\\
f\big\downarrow & & \big\downarrow f' & & \big\downarrow e & &
\big\downarrow e'\\
S & \xleftarrow{\;\;} & S' & \xleftarrow{g} & T & \xleftarrow{\pi} & T'
\end{array}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\begin{array}{ccccc}
X' & &\xleftarrow{h'=h\circ\pi'}& &Y'\\
f'\big\downarrow & & & & \big\downarrow e'\\
S' & &\xleftarrow{g'=g\circ\pi}& &T'
\end{array}
$$

where all squares are Cartesian, $g$ is quasi-compact and
quasi-separated, and $\pi:T'\to T$ is integral surjective. Let
$\mathcal F$ be an abelian sheaf on $T_{\Et}$ annihilated by $n$ and set
$\mathcal F'=\pi^{-1}\mathcal F$. If

$$
f'^{-1}R^qg'_*\mathcal F'\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
R^qh'_*(e')^{-1}\mathcal F'
$$

is an isomorphism, then
$f'^{-1}R^qg_*\mathcal F\to R^qh_*e^{-1}\mathcal F$ is an isomorphism.
(*Stacks Project, [Tag `0F04`](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F04).*)

proof.text: By the universal clause of [sbc-def-base-change-property], $\mathrm{BC}(f\prime,n,q-1)$ holds. The right-hand Cartesian square identifies $\pi\prime:Y\prime\to Y$ as the base change of $\pi$. By [pqf-lem-integral-univclosed], $\pi$ is affine and universally closed. Its base change $\pi\prime$ is affine by [lem-weil-pbc-affine-morphism-permanence] (1), and universally closed by [lem-weil-pbc-universally-closed-base-change]. Apply the reverse implication of [pqf-lem-integral-univclosed] to conclude that $\pi\prime$ is integral. This is a three-line permanence argument from existing statements, not a new node.

Put $\mathcal G=\pi_*\pi^{-1}\mathcal F=\pi_*\mathcal F'$ and let $\eta:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ be the adjunction unit [def-weil-pbc-inverse-image]. For each point $t'\in T'$ choose its algebraic-closure geometric point $\bar t'$ and put $\bar t=\pi\bar t'$. Surjectivity of $\pi$ says that this family of $\bar t$ covers all underlying points of $T$ [def-weil-surjective-morphism]. Define $r_{\bar t'}:\mathcal G_{\bar t}\to\mathcal F'_{\bar t'}$ by sending a germ represented by $b\in\mathcal G(U)=\mathcal F'(U\times_TT')$ at a pointed etale neighbourhood $(U,\bar u)$ of $\bar t$ to the germ of $b$ at $(U\times_TT',(\bar u,\bar t'))$. Here the section formula is [def-weil-pbc-direct-image]. Restriction maps commute with this assignment, so it is well-defined on the stalk colimit. The unit-germ formula of [lem-weil-pbc-inverse-image-stalk-germ] gives $c_{\pi,\bar t',\mathcal F}\circ r_{\bar t'}\circ\eta_{\bar t}=1_{\mathcal F_{\bar t}}$. Hence $\eta_{\bar t}$ has a left inverse. By [lem-weil-pbc-geometric-stalks-detect-mono], $\eta$ is a monomorphism. No finite-stalk product formula is used.

Both $\mathcal F'$ and $\mathcal G$ are annihilated by $n$: inverse image is additive by [prop-weil-pbc-inverse-image-modules-exact], and direct image is additive by [def-weil-pbc-direct-image], so they send the zero endomorphism $n\,1_{\mathcal F}$ to $n\,1_{\mathcal F'}$ and $n\,1_{\mathcal G}$. Apply [sbc-lem-bc-injectivity] (1) and (2) to the given qcqs $g:T\to S'$ and the inclusion $\eta$. Thus the degree-$q$ map for $\mathcal F$ is injective, and its cokernel embeds in the cokernel of the degree-$q$ map for $\mathcal G$. It remains to prove that latter map is an isomorphism.

Apply [lem-sbc-integral-underived-exchange] with $\Lambda=\mathbf Z$ to the square $(\pi,\pi',e,e')$. Its canonical map $\theta:e^{-1}\pi_*\to\pi'_*(e')^{-1}$ is an isomorphism. Both integral direct images are exact and equal their bounded-below derived functors by [sbc-lem-integral-etale-direct-image-exact]; both inverse images are exact by [prop-weil-pbc-inverse-image-modules-exact]. Applying $\theta$ in each degree of a complex therefore gives an isomorphism of complexes (naturality makes it commute with differentials), and [lem-weil-pbc-exact-functor-derived-functor] identifies the four termwise exact functors with their derived functors. In particular the canonical derived exchange $\theta^D_{\mathcal F'}:e^{-1}R\pi_*\mathcal F'\to R\pi'_*(e')^{-1}\mathcal F'$ is an isomorphism. It is the canonical exchange, rather than an arbitrary object isomorphism: its unit and counit formula in [sbc-def-base-change-map], applied to these exact functors, is the same termwise adjunction formula as that for $\theta$, under the canonical derived comparisons.

Using the canonical composition isomorphisms of [lem-weil-pbc-ringed-topoi-derived-pushforward-composition] and $R\pi_*=\pi_*$, $R\pi'_*=\pi'_*$ from [sbc-lem-integral-etale-direct-image-exact], identify $Rg_*\mathcal G$ with $Rg'_*\mathcal F'$ and identify $Rh_*\pi'_*(e')^{-1}\mathcal F'$ with $Rh'_* (e')^{-1}\mathcal F'$. For these applications the sites are the small skeletons fixed by [sbc-def-base-change-map], with constant coefficient ring $\mathbf Z$. No qcqs hypothesis on $h$ or finiteness hypothesis on $\pi$ is needed for derived pushforward composition.

Apply the vertical-pasting identity, clause (3) of [lem-weil-pbc-exchange-identity-pasting], to the two squares with direct-image sides $(g,h)$ and $(\pi,\pi')$ and base-change sides $(f',e)$ and $(e,e')$. Under the composition identifications in step 5 it states $\operatorname{BC}_{f',g'}(\mathcal F')=Rh_*(\theta^D_{\mathcal F'})\circ\operatorname{BC}_{f',g}(R\pi_*\mathcal F')$. The second factor is the derived base-change map at $\mathcal G$, since $R\pi_*\mathcal F'=\mathcal G[0]$. The first factor is an isomorphism by step 4. Take $q$-th cohomology: [sbc-def-base-change-map] identifies these maps with the stated degree-$q$ maps, and [lem-weil-pbc-exact-functor-complex-cohomology] supplies the natural identification through the exact inverse image $(f')^{-1}$. By the hypothesis the left-hand degree-$q$ map is an isomorphism. Since $H^q(Rh_*(\theta^D_{\mathcal F'}))$ is an isomorphism too, the degree-$q$ map for $\mathcal G$ is an isomorphism. This verifies agreement of the actual morphisms, not just agreement of their sources and targets.

The cokernel for $\mathcal G$ is zero by step 6. Its subobject, the cokernel for $\mathcal F$ from step 3, is therefore zero, so the map for $\mathcal F$ is surjective. It is also injective by step 3; hence it is an isomorphism of abelian sheaves, which is the conclusion.
